abstract.para: Snapshots do not differ technically. &snapper; distinguishes them by the event that triggers them and by how it handles them: as a pre and post pair or as a single snapshot, and with which cleanup algorithm.

entry.para: Package changes with zypper or another tool based on libzypp

section.title: Installation snapshots
section.para: When you install, update or remove packages, snapshot behavior depends on the type of your system. Standard systems have a read-write root file system. Immutable systems (also called transactional systems), such as &slm;, use a read-only root file system and are changed with transactional-update.

listitem.para: When you change packages with zypper or another tool based on libzypp (such as PackageKit), a pair of snapshots is created: one before the system change (pre) and one after it (post). Installation snapshots are enabled by default. To disable them, uninstall the package snapper-zypp-plugin.

On immutable systems, no pre and post snapshots are created. Instead, each change (each transactional-update run or zypper) creates a single new snapshot, and you must boot into it for the change to take effect. These snapshots are an essential part of the system and cannot be disabled.

section.para: On both system types, &snapper; marks snapshots that update critical system components (such as the kernel) as important (important=yes in the Userdata column) and deletes old snapshots automatically. By default, up to ten important snapshots and up to ten regular ones are kept.
Installation snapshots are also called numbered snapshots, because &snapper; cleans them up with the number algorithm. See .

section.title: Timeline snapshots
section.para: Timeline snapshots are disabled for the root partition by default. When you enable them, &snapper; creates one snapshot every hour. The snapshots are created by the snapper-timeline.timer &systemd; timer. To change how often snapshots are created, modify this timer, as this cannot be configured within &snapper; itself.

The cleanup of timeline snapshots is based on hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly intervals. By default, &snapper; keeps the last ten hourly snapshots and the first snapshot of each of the last ten days, months and years. It deletes older snapshots automatically.

section.title: Pre, post and single snapshots
section.para: By time of creation, &snapper; recognizes three snapshot types. They do not differ physically, but &snapper; handles them differently.

listitem.para: A snapshot of a file system before a modification. Each pre snapshot corresponds to a post snapshot. For example, this is used for installation snapshots on standard systems.
A snapshot of a file system after a modification. Each post snapshot corresponds to a pre snapshot. For example, this is used for installation snapshots on standard systems.
A stand-alone snapshot. This is the default type when creating snapshots. For example, this is used for timeline snapshots and for installation snapshots on immutable systems.

section.title: Example list of snapshots
section.para: On a standard system, a fresh installation followed by two software changes made through PackageKit looks like this:
section.screen: &prompt.sudo;snapper list # | Type | Pre # | Date | User | Used Space | Cleanup | Description | Userdata --+--------+-------+----------------------------------+------+------------+---------+-----------------------+--------------- 0 | single | | | root | | | current | 1*| single | | Fri 02 Oct 2026 03:26:40 PM CEST | root | 180.88 MiB | | first root filesystem | 2 | pre | | Mon 05 Oct 2026 02:25:42 PM CEST | root | 689.28 MiB | number | zypp(packagekitd) | important=yes 3 | post | 2 | Mon 05 Oct 2026 02:28:19 PM CEST | root | 105.41 MiB | number | | important=yes 4 | pre | | Tue 10 Nov 2026 03:18:44 PM CET | root | 7.41 MiB | number | zypp(packagekitd) | important=yes 5 | post | 4 | Tue 10 Nov 2026 03:19:33 PM CET | root | 31.88 MiB | number | | important=yes
section.para: The asterisk (*) next to a snapshot number marks the snapshot that is currently mounted as the root file system. It is also the default snapshot to boot from.

Snapshot 0 with the description current is not a real snapshot. It always refers to the current state of the running system. The installer creates snapshot 1 with the description first root filesystem. It contains the initial installation of the system. In a post snapshot, the Pre # column shows the number of the matching pre snapshot.
